# Introduction

**Business Problem**

U.S. natural gas consumption forecasting is an important business problem because accurate demand forecasts can support energy planning, infrastructure management, storage and supply decisions, and broader policy analysis. Since natural gas demand is highly seasonal and can change over time, the key question of this project is whether classical time-series methods can produce reliable short- and medium-term forecasts for monthly U.S. total natural gas consumption. 

**This report covers**

- **Experimental results and Analysis**: Understand the overall structure of the monthly natural gas consumption series, identify long-run trend and strong annual seasonality, examine whether the seasonal variation grows with the level of the series, and highlight unusual periods such as major demand shocks or extreme peaks.
- **Variance Stabilization and Diagnostics**: Evaluate whether a Box-Cox transformation is needed to stabilize variance, and use autocorrelation, partial autocorrelation, stationarity testing, and related diagnostics to better understand the dependence structure of the series before modeling.
- **Benchmark Model**: Use the seasonal naïve model as a simple but meaningful benchmark, since monthly natural gas consumption has a strong yearly seasonal cycle. This gives us a baseline forecast to compare against more structured forecasting models. 
- **Regression Model**: Fit a regression model with linear trend and seasonal dummy variables to capture the main deterministic components of the series, then evaluate whether this simple explanatory structure can improve forecast accuracy relative to the benchmark. 
- **ARIMA Modeling**: Build ARIMA-based models to capture both trend-adjusted serial dependence and seasonal correlation in the data, and assess whether modeling the stochastic structure of the series leads to better out-of-sample forecasts. 
- **Exponential Smoothing**: Use HOLT-WINTERS Seasonal Methods to capture level, trend, and seasonality in a flexible forecasting framework, and compare their predictive performance with the regression and ARIMA approaches. 
- **Model Evaluation and Forecast Comparison**: Reserve the final 24 months as a test set, compare all candidate models using out-of-sample forecast accuracy, and determine which method performs best for forecasting future U.S. natural gas consumption. 
- **Final Objective**: Draw a practical conclusion about which classical time-series model is most appropriate for this dataset, and show how time-series forecasting can support real-world decision-making in the U.S. energy sector.

**Train / Test split**: We reserve the last 24 months (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025) as the test set, leaving 216 monthly observations (Jan 2006 – Dec 2023) for training. Using two full seasonal cycles ensures a robust evaluation of forecasting accuracy.

# Data Loading and Preprocessing

## Load Required Libraries

```{r libraries}
library(forecast)    # forecasting models and utilities
library(ggplot2)     # plotting
library(TSA)         # periodogram
library(tseries)     # adf.test, kpss.test
library(lmtest)      # dwtest, bgtest
library(knitr)       # kable
library(kableExtra)  # styled tables
library(gridExtra)   # grid.arrange
```

## Read and Clean the Data

The raw CSV from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) contains 4 header rows of metadata. We skip those, read the two columns, parse dates, and reverse the rows so that the series runs in chronological order.

```{r load-data}
# ---- Read raw CSV (skip 4 metadata rows) ----
raw <- read.csv("./U.S._Natural_Gas_Total_Consumption.csv",
                skip = 4, header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Rename columns for convenience
colnames(raw) <- c("Month", "Consumption")

# Parse the Month column -> Date (first day of each month)
raw$Date <- as.Date(paste0("01 ", raw$Month), format = "%d %b %Y")

# Sort chronologically (original file is in reverse order)
raw <- raw[order(raw$Date), ]

# Quick sanity check
head(raw, 5)
tail(raw, 5)
cat("Total observations in raw file:", nrow(raw), "\n")
```

## Subset to Study Period and Create ts Object

We focus on **January 2006 – December 2025** (240 monthly observations).

```{r create-ts}
# Filter to study period
df <- raw[raw$Date >= as.Date("2006-01-01") & raw$Date <= as.Date("2025-12-31"), ]
cat("Observations in study period:", nrow(df), "\n")

# Build ts object (monthly, starting Jan 2006)
gas_ts <- ts(df$Consumption, start = c(2006, 1), frequency = 12)
```

## Train / Test Split

```{r train-test}
# Last 24 months as test set (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025)
train_ts <- window(gas_ts, end = c(2023, 12))
test_ts  <- window(gas_ts, start = c(2024, 1))

cat("Training set:", length(train_ts), "obs  |  ",
    "Test set:", length(test_ts), "obs\n")
```

Unless otherwise noted, the original EIA monthly series is measured in **million cubic feet**. For readability, plots that divide values by $10^6$ report the vertical axis in **trillion cubic feet**.

# Experimental results and Analysis

## Time Series Visualization

### Time Series Plot

```{r ts-plot, fig.height=5}
autoplot(gas_ts / 1e6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2024, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 2024.3, y = max(gas_ts/1e6)*0.95,
           label = "Train / Test split", color = "red", hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Monthly Natural Gas Total Consumption (2006–2025)",
       subtitle = "Dashed line marks the train/test boundary (Jan 2024)",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:**

- There is a clear **upward trend** over the 20-year period, reflecting growing demand for natural gas in the U.S. driven by the shift from coal to gas-fired power generation and expanding LNG exports.
- A strong **seasonal pattern** is visible: consumption peaks in winter months (December–February) due to heating demand and dips in spring/fall shoulder seasons, creating a distinctive "sawtooth" shape.
- The **amplitude of seasonal fluctuations appears to increase** over time — early years (2006–2010) show winter-summer swings of roughly 1.0–1.2 trillion cubic feet, while recent years (2021–2025) exhibit swings of 1.3–1.5 trillion. This suggests the variance grows with the level, indicating that a **multiplicative** model (or equivalently, a Box-Cox transformation) may be appropriate.
- Notable anomalies include a visible dip around **2020** (COVID-19 pandemic reduced industrial and commercial demand), a relatively sharp winter peak in early **2014** (Polar Vortex events), and a record high near **4.0 trillion cubic feet in January 2025** — the highest single-month value in the entire series.

### Seasonal Subseries Plot

```{r seasonal-subseries, fig.height=5}
ggsubseriesplot(gas_ts / 1e6) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Subseries Plot",
       subtitle = "Horizontal lines show monthly means; within-month trends show year-over-year changes",
       y = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:**

- January is consistently the highest-consumption month (mean ≈ 3.1 trillion cubic feet), followed by December and February — all driven by winter heating demand.
- The lowest consumption occurs in the **shoulder and summer months** (May, June, and September), where means drop to roughly 1.95 trillion cubic feet. Notably, July and August show a **slight rebound** above June and September, reflecting increased gas-fired electricity generation for summer cooling.
- Within nearly every month, there is a clear **upward drift** over the years, confirming the long-term growth trend across all seasons — not just winter.
- The spread (range from min to max) in winter months (especially January, ranging from ~2.5 to ~3.9) is **substantially wider** than in summer months (e.g., June, ranging from ~1.4 to ~2.4), reinforcing the observation of **increasing variance with level** and the need for a variance-stabilizing transformation.

### Seasonal Box Plot

```{r seasonal-boxplot, fig.height=5}
boxplot(gas_ts / 1e6 ~ cycle(gas_ts),
        xlab  = "Month",
        ylab  = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)",
        main  = "Monthly Distribution of Natural Gas Consumption",
        col   = "lightblue",
        names = month.abb)
```

**Interpretation:**

- The boxplot reveals a clear **U-shaped seasonal pattern**: consumption is highest in January (median ≈ 3.1), drops through spring to a trough in September–October (median ≈ 2.0), then rises sharply into the winter months again, with December's median reaching approximately 3.0.
- **Winter months (Jan, Feb, Dec)** show both the highest medians and the **greatest variability** — January's box spans roughly 2.8 to 3.3 with whiskers extending from about 2.2 to 4.0. In contrast, **summer months (Jun–Sep)** have much more compact boxes, indicating lower and more stable consumption.
- January contains a visible **upper outlier** near 4.0 (the record January 2025 value noted earlier), further illustrating the extremes possible in peak heating season.
- The systematic relationship between median level and spread (higher consumption months have wider boxes) confirms that **variance increases with the level** of the series, supporting the Box-Cox transformation decision.

### Time Series Decomposition (STL)

We use STL (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess), which is robust to outliers and allows the seasonal component to change over time.

```{r stl-decomposition, fig.height=7}
stl_decomp <- stl(gas_ts, s.window = "periodic")
autoplot(stl_decomp) +
  ggtitle("STL Decomposition of U.S. Natural Gas Consumption") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Trend:** Shows growth from approximately 1.9 million cubic feet units in 2006 to roughly 2.8 million cubic feet units in 2025. The growth is not entirely steady- there is a noticeable **plateau around 2008–2012** (likely reflecting the impact of the Great Recession on energy demand), followed by sustained growth from 2013 onward, a brief **dip in 2020** (COVID-19), and then a steep acceleration into 2024–2025.
- **Seasonal:** A consistent annual cycle with amplitude of roughly ±500,000–600,000 MCF (note: we used `s.window = "periodic"`, so the seasonal component is constant across all years). The sharp positive peaks correspond to winter months and the troughs to shoulder/summer months, confirming the expected heating-driven seasonal pattern.
- **Remainder:** Mostly centered around zero and random in appearance, but several notable spikes stand out: a large **positive residual near 2014** (Polar Vortex winter), some **negative residuals around 2012 and 2020**, and a very large **positive spike near 2025** (likely January 2025, the record-high month identified earlier). These isolated extremes do not indicate systematic model failure but rather unusual weather-driven demand events.

## Box-Cox Transformation Analysis

When the seasonal amplitude grows proportionally with the level of the series, a **Box-Cox transformation** can stabilize the variance before modeling. The transformation is defined as:

$$y^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \frac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}, & \lambda \neq 0 \\ \log(y), & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}$$

We use `BoxCox.lambda()` (which applies the Guerrero method to minimize the coefficient of variation of the subseries) to find the optimal $\lambda$ value.

### Find Optimal Lambda

```{r boxcox-lambda}
lambda_bc <- BoxCox.lambda(train_ts)
cat("Optimal Box-Cox lambda:", round(lambda_bc, 4), "\n")

# Flag for later use
use_boxcox <- abs(lambda_bc - 1) >= 0.15
```

### Visual Comparison: Original vs. Transformed

```{r boxcox-compare, fig.height=8}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Original series
plot(gas_ts / 1e6, main = "Original Series",
     ylab = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)", xlab = "Year")

# Transformed series
plot(BoxCox(gas_ts, lambda_bc),
     main = paste0("Box-Cox Transformed Series (lambda = ", round(lambda_bc, 2), ")"),
     ylab = "Transformed Consumption", xlab = "Year")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Interpretation & Decision:**

As a general guideline for Box-Cox transformation:

- If $\lambda \approx 1$: no transformation is needed — the variance is already roughly constant across the level of the series.
- If $\lambda \approx 0$: a **log transformation** is appropriate (the Box-Cox formula reduces to $\log(y)$ as $\lambda \to 0$).
- If $\lambda$ takes some other value: apply the **Box-Cox power transformation** $y^{(\lambda)} = \frac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}$ to stabilize variance.

In our case, the common Box-Cox estimate is $\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$, which falls between 0 and 1 - neither close to 1 (no transform) nor close to 0 (log transform). This indicates that a Box-Cox transformation is appropriate. The seasonal amplitude in the original series grows with the level (as observed in the time series plot and seasonal subseries plot), and this transformation compresses larger winter peaks proportionally more than smaller summer values, yielding a more homogeneous variance across time.

### Variance Stabilization Check

To confirm the transformation works, we compare the spread of the data within each year before and after transformation.

```{r variance-check, fig.height=5}
# Compute annual standard deviation as a simple variance check
years <- floor(time(gas_ts))
annual_sd_orig <- tapply(as.numeric(gas_ts), years, sd)
annual_sd_bc   <- tapply(as.numeric(BoxCox(gas_ts, lambda_bc)), years, sd)

yr_orig <- as.numeric(names(annual_sd_orig))
yr_bc   <- as.numeric(names(annual_sd_bc))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Left: Original
plot(yr_orig, annual_sd_orig, type = "b", pch = 16,
     main = "Annual SD: Original",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Standard Deviation")
abline(lm(annual_sd_orig ~ yr_orig), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

# Right: After Box-Cox
plot(yr_bc, annual_sd_bc, type = "b", pch = 16,
     main = "Annual SD: After Box-Cox",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Standard Deviation")
abline(lm(annual_sd_bc ~ yr_bc), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Interpretation:**

- In the left panel (original series), the annual standard deviation ranges from approximately 250,000 to 530,000. The red trend line shows a clear **positive slope**, confirming that the spread of the data increases systematically over time as overall consumption grows.
- In the right panel (after Box-Cox with $\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$), the annual standard deviation ranges from about 1,300 to 2,100, and the red trend line is **nearly flat** - indicating that the transformation has effectively removed the systematic growth in variance. Year-to-year fluctuations remain (driven by unusual weather events like the 2014 Polar Vortex and 2025 winter), but the overall upward drift in variability has been eliminated.
- The contrast between the two trend lines provides clear visual evidence that the Box-Cox transformation successfully stabilizes variance, validating its use for subsequent modeling by all team members.

## ACF and PACF Analysis

We examine the autocorrelation structure of the original series. This is a descriptive step to characterize the data's temporal dependencies as part of EDA.

### ACF of Original Series

```{r acf-original, fig.height=5}
ggAcf(gas_ts, lag.max = 48) +
  ggtitle("ACF of Original Series (up to 48 lags)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:**

- The ACF decays **very slowly**, which is a hallmark of a **non-stationary** series with a strong trend component.
- Clear **peaks at lags 12, 24, 36, 48** indicate strong annual seasonality - observations from the same month in different years are highly correlated.
- The slow decay and seasonal peaks together indicate the series is **non-stationary** and would require differencing to achieve stationarity before applying models that assume stationary input.

### PACF of Original Series

```{r pacf-original, fig.height=5}
ggAcf(gas_ts, lag.max = 48, type = "partial") +
  ggtitle("PACF of Original Series (up to 48 lags)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:**

- The PACF shows a **large spike at lag 1** and a **significant spike at lag 12**, confirming both short-term dependence and seasonal dependence.
- After these dominant lags, the PACF cuts off relatively quickly, suggesting that the series has a low-order autoregressive structure with a seasonal component.

### ACF / PACF of Box-Cox Transformed Series

```{r acf-transformed, fig.height=8}
train_ts_bc <- BoxCox(train_ts, lambda_bc)
p1 <- ggAcf(train_ts_bc, lag.max = 48) +
  ggtitle("ACF of Box-Cox Transformed (Training) Series") + theme_minimal()
p2 <- ggAcf(train_ts_bc, lag.max = 48, type = "partial") +
  ggtitle("PACF of Box-Cox Transformed (Training) Series") + theme_minimal()
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 2)
```

**Interpretation:**

- The overall ACF/PACF patterns remain similar to the original series - slow decay in ACF with seasonal peaks, and dominant PACF spikes at lags 1 and 12. This is expected because the Box-Cox transformation stabilizes **variance**, not the mean structure or autocorrelation.
- The key takeaway is that the temporal dependency structure (trend + seasonality) persists after transformation, confirming that variance stabilization alone is not sufficient to achieve stationarity — differencing would still be required for models that assume stationary input.

## Stationarity Test (Hypothesis Testing)

As a formal confirmation of the non-stationarity observed in the ACF, we apply the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test and the KPSS test.

```{r stationarity-test, results='hold'}
# ADF test: H0 = series has a unit root (non-stationary)
adf_result <- adf.test(gas_ts)
cat("ADF Test:\n")
cat("  Test statistic:", round(adf_result$statistic, 4), "\n")
cat("  p-value:       ", format.pval(adf_result$p.value, digits = 4), "\n\n")

# KPSS test: H0 = series is stationary
kpss_result <- kpss.test(gas_ts, null = "Trend")
cat("KPSS Test (with trend):\n")
cat("  Test statistic:", round(kpss_result$statistic, 4), "\n")
cat("  p-value:       ", format.pval(kpss_result$p.value, digits = 4), "\n")
```

**Interpretation:**

- The **ADF test** (H₀: series has a unit root) and **KPSS test** (H₀: trend-stationary) provide useful but limited guidance in the presence of strong seasonality.
- Therefore, formal tests are interpreted together with visual diagnostics. The original series still shows persistent seasonal dependence and a changing mean structure.
- For ARIMA modeling, seasonal differencing and (if needed) first differencing remain appropriate to remove persistent dependence and stabilize the mean.

The ADF test and KPSS test should be interpreted with caution because the original series exhibits strong seasonality and a clear changing mean structure. In this setting, formal stationarity tests alone do not provide a simple or definitive conclusion about whether the series is fully stationary. Instead, they should be considered together with the time-series plot, decomposition, and autocorrelation diagnostics, all of which show persistent annual dependence and non-constant mean behavior in the original series. Therefore, for ARIMA modeling, it is reasonable to consider seasonal differencing first, and then assess whether additional non-seasonal differencing is needed based on model diagnostics and forecast performance.

## Spectral Analysis

A periodogram helps us identify the dominant frequency components in the series. We expect a strong peak at frequency $f = 1/12$ (the annual cycle).

```{r spectral, fig.height=5}
# Use TSA::periodogram on the training set
p <- periodogram(train_ts, main = "Periodogram of Training Series")
```

```{r spectral-top}
# Identify top frequencies
freq_df <- data.frame(Frequency = p$freq, Spectrum = p$spec)
freq_df <- freq_df[order(-freq_df$Spectrum), ]
top5 <- head(freq_df, 5)
top5$Period_months <- round(1 / top5$Frequency, 1)
print(top5)
```

**Interpretation:**

- The **dominant peak** appears at frequency = 0.0833 (period = **12 months**), confirming the strong annual seasonal cycle driven by winter heating demand.
- The **second-largest peak** occurs near frequency = 0.0046 (period = 216 months, i.e., the full length of the training set), which represents the **long-term trend** component in the data.
- A **third prominent peak** appears at frequency = 0.1667 (period = **6 months**), representing a semi-annual harmonic. This indicates that the seasonal pattern is not a simple sinusoid — there is an asymmetry between the sharp winter peak and the broader summer trough, which produces this second harmonic.

# Benchmark Model: Seasonal Naïve

## Model Specification

The **Seasonal Naïve** method uses the most recent observation from the same season as the forecast:

$$\hat{y}_{t+h} = y_{t + h - m}$$

where $m = 12$ (monthly data). This is the simplest reasonable benchmark for seasonal time series and serves as the baseline for comparing more sophisticated models.

## Model Fitting

Seasonal naive forecasting does not require differencing or Box-Cox transformation. The method simply uses the observation from the same season in the previous cycle as the forecast. Because it directly relies on the seasonal pattern in the data, no transformation is needed to achieve stationarity or stabilize variance.

```{r snaive-fit}
# Fit Seasonal Naïve on training data, forecast h = 24 months ahead
snaive_fit <- snaive(train_ts, h = 24)

# Summary
summary(snaive_fit)
```

## Forecast Visualization

```{r snaive-forecast-plot, fig.height=5}
autoplot(snaive_fit) +
  autolayer(test_ts, series = "Actual", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Naïve Forecast vs. Actual (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025)",
       subtitle = "Blue = Forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals; Red = Actual",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Consumption (Million Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Series"))
```

**Interpretation:**

- The Seasonal Naïve forecast replicates the consumption values from 2023 as the forecasts for both 2024 and 2025 (flat point forecasts repeated each year).
- The actual values (red line) generally track within or near the prediction intervals for 2024. However, in 2025 the forecast cannot capture the year-over-year growth: the actual values consistently exceed the forecasted levels, most notably **January 2025** (actual = 3.92 million vs. forecast = 3.32 million), which breaks above even the **95% prediction interval** upper bound of 3.73 million. This highlights the model's inability to account for the upward trend.
- The positive mean error (ME ≈ 57,814) on the test set confirms this systematic under-prediction, which is expected since the Seasonal Naïve ignores the upward trend.
- This provides a clear motivation for more advanced models that can capture both trend and seasonality.

### Zoomed Forecast Comparison

```{r snaive-zoom, fig.height=5}
# Zoom into the test period for a closer look
autoplot(window(gas_ts, start = c(2021, 1))) +
  autolayer(snaive_fit$mean, series = "Seasonal Naïve", lwd = 1) +
  autolayer(test_ts, series = "Actual", lwd = 1) +
  labs(title = "Zoomed Forecast Comparison (2021–2025)",
       x = "Year", y = "Consumption (Million Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Series"))
```

## Forecast Accuracy

```{r snaive-accuracy}
snaive_acc <- accuracy(snaive_fit, test_ts)
print(round(snaive_acc, 2))
```

```{r snaive-accuracy-table, results='hold'}
# Extract test-set accuracy for clean reporting
snaive_test_acc <- snaive_acc["Test set", ]
cat("\n========================================\n")
cat("  SEASONAL NAIVE - TEST SET PERFORMANCE\n")
cat("========================================\n")
cat("  RMSE  :", format(round(snaive_test_acc["RMSE"]), big.mark = ","), "Million Cubic Feet\n")
cat("  MAE   :", format(round(snaive_test_acc["MAE"]), big.mark = ","), "Million Cubic Feet\n")
cat(sprintf("  MAPE  : %.2f%%\n", snaive_test_acc["MAPE"]))
cat(sprintf("  MASE  : %.4f\n", snaive_test_acc["MASE"]))
cat("========================================\n")
cat("\nNote: These metrics serve as the BASELINE.\n")
cat("All other models should aim to beat these numbers.\n")
```

**Interpretation:**

- **RMSE = 194,709** and **MAE = 123,366** (Million Cubic Feet): These measure absolute forecast error. On average, the Seasonal Naïve forecast is off by about 123 billion cubic feet per month — roughly 4–6% of typical monthly consumption.
- **MAPE = 3.90%**: The average percentage error is relatively low, suggesting the seasonal pattern alone carries strong predictive power. However, this benchmark does not capture trend, so more sophisticated models should improve upon this.
- **MASE = 1.05**: A MASE very close to 1.0 means the test-set performance is comparable to the in-sample seasonal naïve errors. Values above 1 indicate that the model performs slightly worse on the test set than on the training set, which may reflect the growing trend that the model ignores. Any model achieving MASE < 1.05 would outperform this benchmark.

## Residual Diagnostics

### Comprehensive Residual Check

```{r snaive-residual-check, fig.height=7}
checkresiduals(snaive_fit)
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Residual time plot:** The residuals fluctuate around zero without a strong visible trend, though the **magnitude of fluctuations** appears somewhat larger in later years (2018–2023) compared to earlier years, consistent with the increasing variance pattern identified in the EDA.
- **ACF of residuals:** A dominant spike at **lag 1** (≈ 0.33) is clearly significant, along with several other spikes scattered across the first 12 lags. This confirms substantial short-term autocorrelation that the Seasonal Naïve model fails to capture — expected for such a simple benchmark.
- **Histogram:** The residuals are roughly bell-shaped but exhibit a **slight right skew** — the right tail extends to approximately 500,000 while the left tail only reaches about −250,000. This suggests occasional large positive forecast errors (actual far exceeding forecast), likely corresponding to unusually cold winters.
- **Ljung-Box test:** $Q^* = 98.75$, $df = 24$, $p$-value $= 4.9 \times 10^{-11}$. This extremely small p-value strongly rejects the null hypothesis of white noise residuals, confirming that significant autocorrelation remains in the residuals. This is expected — the Seasonal Naïve model is intentionally simple and does not model short-term dependencies or trend.


### Additional Residual Plots

```{r snaive-residual-extras, fig.height=8}
snaive_res <- residuals(snaive_fit)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# 1. Residuals over time
plot(snaive_res, main = "Residuals Over Time", ylab = "Residual", xlab = "Year")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

# 2. QQ Plot
qqnorm(snaive_res, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
qqline(snaive_res, col = "red")

# 3. Histogram with density curve
hist(snaive_res, breaks = 25, freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue",
     main = "Histogram of Residuals", xlab = "Residual")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mean(snaive_res), sd = sd(snaive_res)),
      add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# 4. Residual vs Fitted
plot(fitted(snaive_fit), snaive_res,
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual", pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Q-Q Plot:** The points follow the diagonal line well through the center of the distribution, but noticeable deviations appear in **both tails**. In the upper-right tail, several points curve above the line, indicating that the largest positive residuals are larger than a normal distribution would predict. In the lower-left tail, a few points fall below the line. These deviations suggest **slightly heavier tails** than a normal distribution, though overall the departure is not severe — consistent with the Shapiro-Wilk test failing to reject normality (p = 0.11) below.
- **Residuals vs. Fitted:** At lower fitted values (around 1.5–2.0 million, corresponding to summer months), the residuals cluster tightly around zero. At higher fitted values (around 3.0–3.5 million, corresponding to winter months), the spread of residuals is noticeably wider, with several points exceeding +400,000. This funnel pattern confirms heteroscedasticity - forecast errors are larger when consumption is higher - supporting the use of the common Box-Cox transformation ($\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$).


### Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test

```{r snaive-shapiro, results='hold'}
snaive_shapiro <- shapiro.test(snaive_res)
cat("Shapiro-Wilk test for normality of residuals:\n")
cat("  W-statistic:", round(snaive_shapiro$statistic, 4), "\n")
cat("  p-value:    ", format.pval(snaive_shapiro$p.value, digits = 4), "\n")
if (snaive_shapiro$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  => Residuals are NOT normally distributed (p < 0.05).\n")
} else {
  cat("  => Cannot reject normality (p >= 0.05).\n")
}
```

**Interpretation:**

- The Shapiro-Wilk test yields $W = 0.9888$ with $p$-value $= 0.1106$. Since $p > 0.05$, we **cannot reject the null hypothesis** of normality at the 5% significance level.
- This means the Seasonal Naïve residuals are approximately normally distributed, which is a favorable property for the validity of prediction intervals. However, the Ljung-Box test above clearly showed these residuals are **not white noise** — they are normally distributed but serially correlated, which is the key limitation of this benchmark model.

## Interim Conclusion

The seasonal naive model provides a strong and interpretable benchmark because it preserves the annual seasonal pattern directly. However, it cannot capture the upward trend and leaves substantial autocorrelation in residuals. Therefore, it serves as a baseline rather than a final forecasting model.

---

# Regression Model: Linear Trend with Seasonal Dummies

Regression is one of the simplest forecasting approaches - it models the series as a linear function of deterministic predictors (trend and seasonal dummies) without using autocorrelation. As noted in class, this is a "Type 1" time domain model: *ordinary regression that uses time indices as x-variables*.

From Part 1, we know:

- Strong upward **trend** and **annual seasonality** (12-month cycle).
- **Box-Cox** $\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$ is used to stabilize variance.
- Seasonal Naïve benchmark: RMSE $\approx$ 194,709 | MAPE $\approx$ 3.90% | MASE $\approx$ 1.05.

**Goal:** Fit a regression model with trend + seasonal dummies, evaluate its
residuals (including formal autocorrelation tests), forecast the 24-month test
set, and compare accuracy against the benchmark.

## Model Specification

We use `tslm()` to fit a linear regression with two components:

$$
y_t^{(\lambda)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{m=2}^{12} \gamma_m D_{m,t} + \varepsilon_t
$$

where:

- $t = 1, 2, \ldots, 216$ is the time index (`trend`),
- $D_{m,t}$ are 11 monthly dummy variables (`season`), with January as the reference category,
- $\varepsilon_t$ is the error term (assumed mean zero, constant variance, and uncorrelated).

**Does the Regression Model Need Differencing?**
  
Before fitting the regression model, it is useful to clarify whether differencing is necessary.

The answer is **no**, and the reason connects directly to the distinction between *deterministic trends* and *stochastic trends* covered in Session 2:

- A **deterministic trend** is a fixed, predictable function of time (e.g., $\mu_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$). The series can be written as $Y_t = \mu_t + X_t$, where $X_t$ is a stationary process. In this case, the correct approach is to **estimate and subtract** the trend via regression, this is exactly what `tslm(y ~ trend + season)` does.

- A **stochastic trend** is driven by cumulative random shocks (e.g., a random walk $Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t$). Differencing ($\nabla Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-1}$) is the appropriate tool to remove this type of trend, and it is the foundation of the ARIMA approach (Part 3).

For our natural gas data, the upward trend has a clear economic explanation (coal-to-gas switching, growing LNG exports) and the seasonal pattern is driven by predictable weather cycles. The regression model treats both as deterministic components and estimates them directly. Differencing would actually be harmful here: it would remove information that the regression model can exploit, and applying both regression on trend *and* differencing would constitute over-correction.

```{r reg-fit}
reg_fit <- tslm(train_ts ~ trend + season, lambda = lambda_bc)
summary(reg_fit)
```

**Interpretation of key coefficients:**

- **Intercept ($\beta_0$)**: This is the estimated baseline level for January (the reference month) at time $t = 0$. Since we are modeling on the Box-Cox transformed scale, the raw coefficient value is not directly interpretable in physical units, but the relative magnitudes across seasonal dummies are meaningful.
- **`trend` ($\beta_1$)**: The positive coefficient confirms the upward trend - each additional month adds a small but consistent increase to the transformed consumption level. Over 216 months, this accumulates to a substantial growth, consistent with the upward trend identified in Part 1's EDA.
- **`season` dummies ($\gamma_2, \ldots, \gamma_{12}$)**: Each coefficient measures that month's deviation from January. Negative coefficients for spring/summer months (especially season6 through season9, corresponding to June–September) reflect the summer trough when heating demand drops. Coefficients near zero for season2 (February) and season12 (December) indicate consumption levels close to January - the three peak winter months. This U-shaped seasonal pattern is consistent with the seasonal boxplot in Part 1.
- **$R^2$**: Indicates the proportion of variance in the transformed series explained by the linear trend and seasonal dummies together. For monthly energy data with strong seasonality, we expect a high $R^2$, but a high $R^2$ does **not** guarantee good forecasting performance - residual autocorrelation can still degrade prediction intervals.

## Model Fitting

```{r reg-fitted-plot, fig.height=5}
autoplot(train_ts / 1e6, series = "Actual (Training)") +
  autolayer(fitted(reg_fit) / 1e6, series = "Regression Fitted") +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies: Fitted vs. Actual",
       subtitle = "Back-transformed to original scale (Trillion Cubic Feet)",
       x = "Year", y = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual (Training)" = "grey50",
                                  "Regression Fitted"  = "steelblue")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Series"))
```

**Interpretation:** The fitted values (blue) track the overall seasonal shape and upward trend well, confirming the model captures the two dominant deterministic components. However, notice that the fitted curve is smooth and repetitive, it repeats the same seasonal pattern every year while the actual data (grey) shows year-to-year irregularities (e.g., the 2014 Polar Vortex spike, the 2020 COVID dip). These deviations end up in the residuals and represent the information that the regression model cannot capture.

## Residual Diagnostics

A good regression model should have residuals that are: (1) mean zero, (2) homoscedastic, (3) approximately normal, and (4) **uncorrelated**. For time series data, checking for autocorrelation in the residuals is especially important, it tells us whether the model has captured all the temporal structure in the data.

### Comprehensive Residual Check

```{r reg-residual-check, fig.height=7}
checkresiduals(reg_fit)
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Residuals over time** (top panel): The residuals fluctuate around zero without a visible trend, suggesting the linear trend term is adequate. However, there are clusters of positive or negative residuals (e.g., several consecutive negative values around 2020), which is a visual sign of autocorrelation.
- **ACF of residuals** (bottom-left): Significant spikes beyond the blue dashed 95% confidence bands indicate leftover autocorrelation. A prominent spike at **lag 1** is typical for regression on time series — nearby months tend to have similar deviations from the fitted seasonal pattern. Spikes at **lags 12 and 24** suggest remaining seasonal autocorrelation that the fixed seasonal dummies did not fully absorb.
- **Histogram** (bottom-right): The distribution is approximately bell-shaped and centred on zero, which is favorable for prediction intervals.
- **Ljung-Box test** (printed below the plot): A small p-value rejects the null hypothesis of white noise residuals, formally confirming that significant autocorrelation remains. This is expected — as discussed in Session 2, regression models on time series data almost always have autocorrelated residuals because they do not model serial dependence.

### Extended Residual Plots

```{r reg-residual-plots, fig.height=8}
reg_res <- residuals(reg_fit)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# 1. Residuals over time
plot(reg_res, main = "Residuals Over Time",
     ylab = "Residual", xlab = "Year")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

# 2. Normal Q-Q Plot
qqnorm(reg_res, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
qqline(reg_res, col = "red")

# 3. Histogram with normal curve
hist(reg_res, breaks = 25, freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue",
     main = "Histogram of Residuals", xlab = "Residual")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mean(reg_res), sd = sd(reg_res)),
      add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# 4. Residuals vs. Fitted Values
plot(fitted(reg_fit), reg_res,
     main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted (transformed scale)",
     ylab = "Residual", pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Q-Q plot** (top-right): The central portion follows the diagonal line well, indicating approximate normality in the bulk of the distribution. Departures appear in both tails, a few large positive residuals in the upper tail (likely from extreme cold-weather demand spikes like the 2014 Polar Vortex and January 2025 record) and slight departures in the lower tail. These are isolated events rather than systematic violations.
- **Residuals vs. Fitted** (bottom-right): The scatter is roughly random with no strong funnel pattern, suggesting the Box-Cox transformation ($\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$) has successfully stabilized the variance. If a clear funnel (increasing spread from left to right) were present, it would indicate heteroscedasticity requiring further transformation.

### Detecting Autocorrelation: Durbin-Watson and Breusch-Godfrey Tests

- **Durbin-Watson test**: Tests for lag-1 autocorrelation in regression residuals. Under $H_0$: $\phi = 0$ (model errors uncorrelated); the test statistic is symmetric around 2 when there is no autocorrelation. Values significantly below 2 indicate positive autocorrelation.
- **Breusch-Godfrey test**: Tests for higher-order serial correlation (up to a specified lag). It is specifically designed for regression models and is more powerful than Durbin-Watson for detecting autocorrelation beyond lag 1. We test up to order 12 to check for residual seasonal autocorrelation.

```{r reg-dw-bg-tests, results='hold'}
# Durbin-Watson test (lag-1 autocorrelation)
dw_result <- dwtest(reg_fit)

cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("  Durbin-Watson Test (H0: no lag-1 autocorrelation)\n")
cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("  DW statistic:", round(dw_result$statistic, 4), "\n")
cat("  p-value:     ", format.pval(dw_result$p.value, digits = 4), "\n")
if (dw_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  => REJECT H0: significant positive autocorrelation at lag 1.\n")
} else {
  cat("  => Cannot reject H0: no evidence of lag-1 autocorrelation.\n")
}

cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("  Breusch-Godfrey Test (H0: no autocorrelation up to lag 12)\n")
cat("=======================================================\n")

# Breusch-Godfrey test (higher-order autocorrelation, up to lag 12)
bg_result <- bgtest(reg_fit, order = 12)

cat("  LM statistic:", round(bg_result$statistic, 4), "\n")
cat("  df:          ", bg_result$parameter, "\n")
cat("  p-value:     ", format.pval(bg_result$p.value, digits = 4), "\n")
if (bg_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  => REJECT H0: significant autocorrelation up to lag 12.\n")
} else {
  cat("  => Cannot reject H0: no evidence of higher-order autocorrelation.\n")
}
cat("=======================================================\n")
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Durbin-Watson**: The DW statistic is well below 2, and the extremely small p-value strongly rejects $H_0$. This confirms **positive autocorrelation at lag 1** — consecutive residuals tend to have the same sign, meaning the regression model systematically over- or under-predicts for stretches of time.
- **Breusch-Godfrey**: The extremely small p-value confirms significant autocorrelation up to lag 12, indicating that seasonal serial correlation also remains in the residuals.
- **Key takeaway**: As discussed in Session 2, forecasts from a model with autocorrelated errors are still **unbiased** (the point forecasts are not "wrong"), but the prediction intervals will be **wider than necessary** because the model fails to exploit the predictable autocorrelation structure. This is the primary motivation for ARIMA models (Part 3), which explicitly model the autocorrelation in the residuals, and for Exponential Smoothing (Part 4), which adaptively weights recent observations.

### Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test

```{r reg-shapiro, results='hold'}
reg_shapiro <- shapiro.test(as.numeric(reg_res))
cat("Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test:\n")
cat("  W =", round(reg_shapiro$statistic, 4),
    "  p-value =", format.pval(reg_shapiro$p.value, digits = 4), "\n")
if (reg_shapiro$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  => Residuals are NOT normally distributed (p < 0.05).\n")
  cat("     Prediction intervals should be interpreted with caution.\n")
} else {
  cat("  => Cannot reject normality (p >= 0.05).\n")
  cat("     This supports the validity of prediction intervals.\n")
}
```

The Shapiro-Wilk test rejects the null hypothesis of normally distributed residuals (p = 0.0107). This suggests that the residuals deviate slightly from normality. While this does not strongly affect point forecasts, it implies that prediction intervals based on the normality assumption should be interpreted with caution. However, the more important diagnostic issue in this model is the presence of significant autocorrelation in the residuals.



## Forecast Visualization

### Generate 24-Month Forecast

The `forecast()` function automatically extrapolates the `trend` and `season` terms into the future.

```{r reg-forecast}
# Forecast 24 months ahead (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025) on transformed scale
reg_fc <- forecast(reg_fit, h = 24)

# Back-transform to original scale
reg_fc_mean  <- reg_fc$mean
reg_fc_lo80  <- reg_fc$lower[, 1]
reg_fc_hi80  <- reg_fc$upper[, 1]
reg_fc_lo95  <- reg_fc$lower[, 2]
reg_fc_hi95  <- reg_fc$upper[, 2]

reg_fc_ts <- ts(reg_fc_mean, start = c(2024, 1), frequency = 12)
```


### Forecast Plot

```{r reg-forecast-plot, fig.height=5}
# Data frame for prediction interval ribbons
ribbon_df <- data.frame(
  x    = as.numeric(time(test_ts)),
  lo80 = as.numeric(reg_fc_lo80 / 1e6),
  hi80 = as.numeric(reg_fc_hi80 / 1e6),
  lo95 = as.numeric(reg_fc_lo95 / 1e6),
  hi95 = as.numeric(reg_fc_hi95 / 1e6)
)

autoplot(window(gas_ts / 1e6, start = c(2018, 1))) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ribbon_df, aes(x = x, ymin = lo95, ymax = hi95),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ribbon_df, aes(x = x, ymin = lo80, ymax = hi80),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  autolayer(reg_fc_ts / 1e6, series = "Regression Forecast", lwd = 1.2) +
  autolayer(test_ts / 1e6, series = "Actual (Test)", lwd = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2024, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(title    = "Regression Forecast vs. Actual (2018–2025)",
       subtitle = "Shaded: 80% (dark) & 95% (light) prediction intervals",
       x = "Year", y = "Consumption (Trillion Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Series"))
```

**Interpretation:** The regression forecast (blue line) captures the seasonal shape and overall level reasonably well. The prediction intervals are quite wide, this is a direct consequence of the autocorrelated residuals detected by the Durbin-Watson and Breusch-Godfrey tests. Because the model does not exploit the serial correlation structure, it treats all residual variation as unpredictable noise, inflating the interval width. A model that accounts for autocorrelation (e.g., ARIMA) would likely produce tighter intervals.


## Forecast Accuracy

### Model Fit: AICc

AICc (corrected Akaike Information Criterion) is a standard metric for comparing models that balances goodness-of-fit against model complexity. It is applicable to any model estimated via maximum likelihood, including linear regression, and penalizes overfitting more heavily in small samples. We report it here as a reference point for cross-model comparison with ARIMA and Holt-Winters models.

**Note:** AICc values are only comparable between models fitted on the **same data and same scale**. Since we fit on the Box-Cox transformed training set, AICc from this regression model can be directly compared with ARIMA and Holt-Winters models that are also fit on the same transformed data.

```{r reg-aicc, results='hold'}
reg_aicc <- reg_fit$call  # for reference
cat("Regression Model AICc:", round(CV(reg_fit)["AICc"], 2), "\n")
cat("(Computed on Box-Cox transformed training data, lambda =",
    round(lambda_bc, 4), ")\n")
cat("\nNote: This value serves as a reference for cross-model\n")
cat("comparison with ARIMA (Part 3) and ETS (Part 4).\n")
```

### Compute Test-Set Accuracy

```{r reg-accuracy}
# Regression model: compute error manually on original scale
# (accuracy() with two plain ts objects returns a named vector, not a matrix)
reg_errors <- as.numeric(test_ts) - as.numeric(reg_fc_ts)
reg_rmse <- sqrt(mean(reg_errors^2))
reg_mae  <- mean(abs(reg_errors))
reg_mape <- mean(abs(reg_errors / as.numeric(test_ts))) * 100

# MASE: scale by in-sample seasonal naïve MAE (same denominator as snaive)
# The seasonal naïve in-sample MAE is the average |y_t - y_{t-12}|
train_vals  <- as.numeric(train_ts)
naive_diffs <- abs(train_vals[13:length(train_vals)] -
                   train_vals[1:(length(train_vals) - 12)])
q <- mean(naive_diffs)
reg_mase <- reg_mae / q

# Combine into named vectors
sn_test  <- snaive_test_acc[c("RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE", "MASE")]
reg_test <- c(RMSE = reg_rmse, MAE = reg_mae, MAPE = reg_mape, MASE = reg_mase)

acc_table <- rbind(
  "Seasonal Naïve (Benchmark)"  = round(sn_test,  2),
  "Regression (Trend + Season)" = round(reg_test, 2)
)

kable(acc_table,
      caption = "Test-Set Accuracy: Regression vs. Seasonal Naïve Benchmark",
      col.names = c("RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE (%)", "MASE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(1, background = "#f5c6cb") %>%
  row_spec(which.min(acc_table[, "RMSE"]),
           bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "steelblue") %>%
  footnote(general = "Pink = benchmark. Blue = best model (lowest RMSE). MASE < 1 means better than seasonal naïve.")
```

## Interim Conclusion

```{r reg-summary-block, results='hold'}
cat("The regression model captures the main deterministic structure through a linear trend and fixed monthly effects.\n")
cat("However, residual diagnostics (Ljung-Box, Durbin-Watson, and Breusch-Godfrey) indicate remaining serial dependence.\n")
cat("Therefore, the model is interpretable and useful, but not sufficient as the final forecasting model.\n")
```

# ARIMA Model

## Model Specification

A general SARIMA model can be written as

$$
\Phi_p(B)\Phi_P(B^{12})(1-B)^d(1-B^{12})^D y_t
=
\Theta_q(B)\Theta_Q(B^{12})\varepsilon_t
$$

where $B$ is the backshift operator, $d$ and $D$ denote the non-seasonal and seasonal differences, and $p,q,P,Q$ represent the orders of the AR and MA components.

Based on the ACF and PACF patterns, the series shows strong seasonal dependence with period 12 and non-stationarity in the mean. 
Therefore, a seasonal difference (D = 1) and possibly a non-seasonal difference (d = 0 or 1) are considered.

The autocorrelation patterns suggest that models including MA and seasonal MA components may be appropriate candidates for SARIMA modeling.

```{r arima-diff-orders}
# suggested differencing orders
d_suggest <- ndiffs(train_ts)
D_suggest <- nsdiffs(train_ts, m = 12)

cat("Suggested non-seasonal differences d =", d_suggest, "\n")
cat("Suggested seasonal differences D =", D_suggest, "\n")
```

```{r arima-seasonal-diff-plot}
# inspect seasonally differenced / fully differenced versions
train_seasdiff <- diff(train_ts, lag = 12)
train_fulldiff <- diff(train_seasdiff, differences = 1)

autoplot(train_seasdiff) +
  ggtitle("Seasonally Differenced Series (lag 12)") +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Seasonal difference")
```

After applying seasonal differencing with lag 12, the strong yearly seasonal pattern is largely removed. The series fluctuates around zero, suggesting that the seasonal component has been reduced.

```{r arima-seasonal-diff-acf}
ggAcf(na.omit(train_seasdiff), lag.max = 60) +
  ggtitle("ACF: Seasonal Difference Only")
```


```{r arima-seasonal-diff-pacf}
ggPacf(na.omit(train_seasdiff), lag.max = 60) +
  ggtitle("PACF: Seasonal Difference Only")
```

The ACF and PACF plots still show significant spikes at early lags, indicating that some short-term dependence remains in the series. 
Therefore, an additional first difference (d = 1) is applied.

```{r arima-full-diff-plot}
autoplot(train_fulldiff) +
  ggtitle("Seasonal + First Differenced Series") +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Differenced series")
```

```{r arima-full-diff-acf}
ggAcf(na.omit(train_fulldiff), lag.max = 60) +
  ggtitle("ACF: Seasonal + First Difference")
```

```{r arima-full-diff-pacf}
ggPacf(na.omit(train_fulldiff), lag.max = 60) +
  ggtitle("PACF: Seasonal + First Difference")
```

```{r arima-adf}
# formal tests (supporting evidence only)
cat("\nADF on Box-Cox train:\n")
print(adf.test(train_ts_bc))
```

```{r arima-kpss}
cat("\nKPSS on Box-Cox train:\n")
print(kpss.test(train_ts_bc, null = "Trend"))
```

The ADF and KPSS outputs should be interpreted together with visual diagnostics. Given the strong seasonal dependence and changing mean structure in the original series, seasonal differencing and (if needed) first differencing remain appropriate for ARIMA modeling.

Based on this evidence, SARIMA structures with seasonal differencing are considered as candidates.

## Candidate Model Selection

```{r arima-candidate-fits}
# Candidate SARIMA models
# For this dataset, start with D = 1 and try d = 0 / 1.

arima_candidate_specs <- list(
  list(order = c(0,0,1), seasonal = c(0,1,1)),
  list(order = c(1,0,0), seasonal = c(1,1,0)),
  list(order = c(1,0,1), seasonal = c(0,1,1)),
  list(order = c(1,0,1), seasonal = c(1,1,0)),
  list(order = c(0,1,1), seasonal = c(0,1,1)),
  list(order = c(1,1,0), seasonal = c(1,1,0)),
  list(order = c(1,1,1), seasonal = c(0,1,1)),
  list(order = c(1,1,1), seasonal = c(1,1,0))
)

fit_candidate <- function(spec, y, lambda_bc) {
  fit <- Arima(
    y,
    order = spec$order,
    seasonal = list(order = spec$seasonal, period = 12),
    lambda = lambda_bc,
    method = "ML"
  )
  return(fit)
}

arima_candidate_fits <- lapply(arima_candidate_specs, fit_candidate, y = train_ts, lambda_bc = lambda_bc)
```

### AICc Comparison

```{r arima-aicc-table}
aicc_tbl <- data.frame(
  model = sapply(seq_along(arima_candidate_specs), function(i) {
    paste0("ARIMA(",
           paste(arima_candidate_specs[[i]]$order, collapse = ","),
           ")(",
           paste(arima_candidate_specs[[i]]$seasonal, collapse = ","),
           ")[12]")
  }),
  AICc = sapply(arima_candidate_fits, function(x) x$aicc),
  AIC  = sapply(arima_candidate_fits, AIC),
  BIC  = sapply(arima_candidate_fits, BIC)
)

aicc_tbl <- aicc_tbl[order(aicc_tbl$AICc), ]
print(aicc_tbl)
```

We first compared several candidate SARIMA models using AICc on the training set. Among all models, ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)[12] achieved the lowest AICc (3737.251), outperforming the remaining candidates. The second-best model, ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)[12], had an AICc about 10 points higher, suggesting that the selected model provides a materially better trade-off between goodness-of-fit and model complexity. Therefore, we retained ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)[12] as the leading candidate and proceeded to validate it using rolling-origin cross-validation and residual diagnostics.

```{r arima-cv-setup}
h <- 12   

fc_fun <- function(y, h, spec, lambda_bc) {
  fit <- Arima(
    y,
    order = spec$order,
    seasonal = list(order = spec$seasonal, period = 12),
    lambda = lambda_bc,
    method = "ML"
  )
  forecast(fit, h = h)
}

```


```{r arima-cv}
arima_cv_results <- data.frame()

for (i in seq_along(arima_candidate_specs)) {
  spec <- arima_candidate_specs[[i]]

  e <- tsCV(
    train_ts,
    forecastfunction = function(y, h) fc_fun(y, h, spec, lambda_bc),
    h = h
  )

  rmse <- sqrt(mean(e^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  mae  <- mean(abs(e), na.rm = TRUE)
  mape <- mean(abs(e / train_ts), na.rm = TRUE) * 100

  model_name <- paste0("ARIMA(",
                       paste(spec$order, collapse = ","),
                       ")(",
                       paste(spec$seasonal, collapse = ","),
                       ")[12]")

  arima_cv_results <- rbind(arima_cv_results,
                      data.frame(model = model_name,
                                 CV_RMSE = rmse,
                                 CV_MAE = mae,
                                 CV_MAPE = mape))
}

arima_cv_results <- arima_cv_results[order(arima_cv_results$CV_RMSE), ]
print(arima_cv_results)
```

Although ARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)[12] achieved the lowest AICc, the simpler model ARIMA(0,0,1)(0,1,1)[12] produced the lowest cross-validation RMSE. Therefore, this model was selected as the final forecasting model.

```{r}
auto.arima(train_ts, lambda=lambda_bc)
```

The `auto.arima()` aligns with our choice.


## Final Model Fitting

```{r arima-final-fit}
# Final model
arima_best_spec <- arima_candidate_specs[[which.min(arima_cv_results$CV_RMSE)]]

arima_fit <- Arima(
  train_ts,
  order = arima_best_spec$order,
  seasonal = list(order = arima_best_spec$seasonal, period = 12),
  lambda = lambda_bc,
  method = "ML"
)

summary(arima_fit)
```

The selected model is SARIMA(0,0,1)(0,1,1)[12] with the common Box-Cox transformation ($\lambda = `r round(lambda_bc, 4)`$). Both the MA(1) and seasonal MA(1) coefficients are statistically significant, indicating that short-term and seasonal error dependencies are captured by the model.

## Residual Diagnostics

```{r arima-residual-check}
# residual diagnostics
checkresiduals(arima_fit)
arima_res <- residuals(arima_fit)
```

The residual time plot shows that the residuals fluctuate around zero without an obvious trend, indicating that the model captures the main structure of the series. The histogram of residuals is approximately symmetric and roughly follows a normal distribution.

Overall, the SARIMA(0,0,1)(0,1,1)[12] model provides a reasonable fit and captures the main seasonal dynamics of the series, although the Ljung–Box test indicates that some residual dependence still remain.

## Forecast Visualization
```{r arima-forecast-plot}
# Forecast on the 24-month test set
arima_fc <- forecast(arima_fit, h = length(test_ts))

autoplot(arima_fc) +
  autolayer(test_ts, series = "Actual") +
  ggtitle("Final SARIMA Forecast vs Actual (Test Set)") +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Consumption")
```

The forecast generally follows the seasonal pattern observed in the actual test data. Although some peaks and troughs are not perfectly captured, the model tracks the overall trend and seasonality reasonably well.

## Forecast Accuracy

```{r arima-accuracy}
arima_acc <- accuracy(arima_fc, test_ts)
print(arima_acc)
```

## Interim Conclusion

The ARIMA model captures short-run and seasonal dependence more explicitly than the regression model. Forecast performance is competitive and aligned with the autocorrelation structure observed in EDA. However, residual diagnostics still indicate remaining dependence, so the model is reasonable but not perfect.

# Exponential Smoothing: HOLT-WINTERS SEASONAL METHOD

## Model Specification

We use `hw()` to fit a Holt-Winters exponential smoothing model. This method is designed for time series with both trend and seasonality, and it decomposes the series into three components: level, trend, and seasonal pattern. For monthly data, the seasonal period is $m = 12$.

For the additive Holt-Winters form, the model can be written as

$$
y_t = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + s_{t-m} + \varepsilon_t
$$

where:

* $y_t$ is the observed value at time $t$,
* $\ell_t$ is the level component,
* $b_t$ is the trend component,
* $s_t$ is the seasonal component,
* $m$ is the seasonal period (for monthly data, $m = 12$),
* $\varepsilon_t$ is the error term.

The components are updated recursively using exponential smoothing equations:

$$
\ell_t = \alpha (y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})
$$

$$
b_t = \beta (\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)b_{t-1}
$$

$$
s_t = \gamma (y_t - \ell_t) + (1-\gamma)s_{t-m}
$$

where $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are the smoothing parameters for the level, trend, and seasonal components, respectively.

When multiplicative seasonality is used, the model instead assumes that seasonal fluctuations scale with the overall level of the series, which is often more appropriate when seasonal variation increases as the series grows over time. In our analysis, we use `hw()` to compare additive versus multiplicative seasonality, as well as damped versus non-damped trend, and select the final specification based on out-of-sample forecast performance.


## Candidate Method Selection

We compare Holt-Winters models within a single model-selection stage. Specifically, we evaluate alternative specifications by varying the seasonal form, the trend damping option, and the use of Box-Cox transformation when applicable. This allows us to determine the most appropriate seasonal structure, assess whether trend damping improves forecast performance, and examine whether variance stabilization helps for additive specifications. We do not consider exponential trend, since the STL decomposition in the previous section suggests that the long-run trend is approximately linear. We also do not apply Box-Cox transformation to multiplicative seasonal models, because this combination is not supported in the underlying implementation of `hw()`.

Therefore, we compare the following candidate models:

- Linear trend with additive seasonality and non-damped
- Linear trend with additive seasonality and damped
- Linear trend with additive seasonality, non-damped, and Box-Cox transformation
- Linear trend with additive seasonality, damped, and Box-Cox transformation
- Linear trend with multiplicative seasonality and non-damped
- Linear trend with multiplicative seasonality and damped

```{r}
hw_add_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "additive", damped = FALSE, h = length(test_ts))
hw_add_damped_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "additive", damped = TRUE,  h = length(test_ts))
hw_add_bc_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "additive", damped = FALSE, h = length(test_ts), lambda = lambda_bc)
hw_add_damped_bc_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "additive", damped = TRUE,  h = length(test_ts), lambda = lambda_bc)
hw_mul_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "multiplicative", damped = FALSE, h = length(test_ts))
hw_mul_damped_fit <- hw(train_ts, seasonal = "multiplicative", damped = TRUE,  h = length(test_ts))
```

```{r}
hw_table <- rbind(
  HW_Add = c(
    AICc = hw_add_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_add_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_add_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_add_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  ),
  HW_Add_Damped = c(
    AICc = hw_add_damped_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_add_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_add_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_add_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  ),
    HW_Add_BC = c(
    AICc = hw_add_bc_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_add_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_add_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_add_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  ),
  HW_Add_Damped_BC = c(
    AICc = hw_add_damped_bc_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_add_damped_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_add_damped_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_add_damped_bc_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  ),
  HW_Mul = c(
    AICc = hw_mul_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_mul_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_mul_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_mul_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  ),
  HW_Mul_Damped = c(
    AICc = hw_mul_damped_fit$model$aicc,
    RMSE = accuracy(hw_mul_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "RMSE"],
    MAE  = accuracy(hw_mul_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAE"],
    MAPE = accuracy(hw_mul_damped_fit, test_ts)[2, "MAPE"]
  )
)

# Find best model by lowest RMSE
best_row <- which.min(hw_table[, "RMSE"])

# Display table
kable(
  hw_table,
  caption = "Holt-Winters Model Comparison",
  col.names = c("AICc", "RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE (%)")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  ) %>%
  row_spec(
    best_row,
    bold = TRUE,
    color = "white",
    background = "steelblue"
  ) %>%
  footnote(
    general = "Blue indicates the best model based on the lowest test-set RMSE. AICc is reported as a supplementary in-sample metric."
  )
```

**Interpretation:**

Among all candidate Holt-Winters specifications, `HW_Mul` performed best overall. It achieved the lowest RMSE (138,222.9), the lowest MAE (102,544.9), and the lowest MAPE (3.679), indicating the strongest out-of-sample forecast accuracy among all models considered. It also had the lowest AICc within the non-Box-Cox models, further supporting its selection as the final Holt-Winters specification.

The additive models generally performed worse than the multiplicative models, suggesting that the seasonal variation is better represented as proportional to the level of the series rather than constant in absolute size. This is consistent with the earlier visual evidence that seasonal fluctuations become larger as the overall series level increases over time.

Trend damping did not improve performance for the multiplicative specification. In fact, `HW_Mul_Damped` was clearly worse than `HW_Mul` across all evaluation metrics, which suggests that the trend in this series should be modeled as continuing rather than gradually flattening. For the additive models, damping slightly improved RMSE and MAE, but the gains were not enough to make the additive family competitive with the best multiplicative model.

Applying a Box-Cox transformation substantially reduced AICc for the additive models, but it did not lead to better forecast accuracy than `HW_Mul`. Although `HW_Add_Damped_BC` was the best-performing additive specification in terms of RMSE and MAE within the additive family, it still remained worse than `HW_Mul` on all out-of-sample accuracy measures. **Therefore, we select the non-damped multiplicative Holt-Winters model as the final model.**


## Final Model Fitting

```{r}
hw_best_spec <- "HW_Mul"
hw_best_fc   <- hw_mul_fit
hw_best_acc  <- accuracy(hw_best_fc, test_ts)["Test set", ]

# Relative change vs seasonal naive baseline (positive = improvement)
rmse_change_pct <- 100 * (snaive_test_acc["RMSE"] - hw_best_acc["RMSE"]) / snaive_test_acc["RMSE"]
mae_change_pct  <- 100 * (snaive_test_acc["MAE"]  - hw_best_acc["MAE"])  / snaive_test_acc["MAE"]
mape_change_pct <- 100 * (snaive_test_acc["MAPE"] - hw_best_acc["MAPE"]) / snaive_test_acc["MAPE"]
mase_change_pct <- 100 * (snaive_test_acc["MASE"] - hw_best_acc["MASE"]) / snaive_test_acc["MASE"]
```


```{r results='hold'}
change_label <- function(x) {
  if (x >= 0) {
    sprintf("improved by %.2f%%", x)
  } else {
    sprintf("worse by %.2f%%", abs(x))
  }
}

cat("\n========================================\n")
cat("   HOLT-WINTERS (HW) - TEST SET\n")
cat("========================================\n")
cat("  Selected candidate:", hw_best_spec, "\n")
cat("  Selected model    : Multiplicative seasonality, non-damped trend\n")
cat("  AICc              :", round(hw_best_fc$model$aicc, 3), "\n")
cat("  RMSE              :", format(round(hw_best_acc["RMSE"]), big.mark = ","), "Million Cubic Feet\n")
cat("  MAE               :", format(round(hw_best_acc["MAE"]), big.mark = ","), "Million Cubic Feet\n")
cat(sprintf("  MAPE              : %.2f%%\n", hw_best_acc["MAPE"]))
cat(sprintf("  MASE              : %.4f\n", hw_best_acc["MASE"]))
cat("\n  Compared with Seasonal Naive:\n")
cat("    RMSE :", change_label(rmse_change_pct), "\n")
cat("    MAE  :", change_label(mae_change_pct), "\n")
cat("    MAPE :", change_label(mape_change_pct), "\n")
cat("    MASE :", change_label(mase_change_pct), "\n")
cat("========================================\n")
```

**Interpretation:**

The final Holt-Winters model selected is `HW_Mul`, which uses multiplicative seasonality with a non-damped trend. This specification achieved the best overall forecasting performance on the test set, with an RMSE of 138,223, an MAE of 102,545, a MAPE of 3.68%, and a MASE of 0.8735. These results indicate that the model provides strong predictive accuracy for the held-out period.

Compared with the seasonal naïve benchmark, the Holt-Winters model shows clear improvement across all evaluation metrics. In particular, RMSE decreased by 29.01%, MAE decreased by 16.88%, MAPE decreased by 5.58%, and MASE also improved by 16.88%. Since the MASE is below 1, this further confirms that the selected model outperforms the seasonal naïve benchmark in forecasting accuracy.

Substantively, these results suggest that the time series is better characterized by multiplicative seasonality rather than additive seasonality, meaning that seasonal fluctuations tend to scale with the overall level of the series. In addition, the non-damped trend performs better than the damped alternative, which implies that allowing the trend to continue without gradual flattening is more appropriate for this dataset. Overall, the selected Holt-Winters model captures the main trend and seasonal structure effectively and provides a meaningful improvement over a simple benchmark forecast.


## Forecast Visualization

```{r}
autoplot(hw_best_fc, series = "Forecast") +
  autolayer(test_ts, series = "Actual") +
  labs(title = "Best Holt-Winters Forecast vs. Actual (Jan 2024 – Dec 2025)",
       subtitle = "Selected model: Multiplicative seasonality, non-damped trend",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Consumption (Million Cubic Feet)",
       colour = "Series") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Forecast" = "blue", "Actual" = "red")) +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r}
autoplot(window(gas_ts, start = c(2021, 1))) +
  autolayer(snaive_fit$mean, series = "Seasonal Naïve", lwd = 1) +
  autolayer(hw_best_fc$mean, series = "Best Holt-Winters", lwd = 1) +
  autolayer(test_ts, series = "Actual", lwd = 1) +
  labs(title = "Zoomed Forecast Comparison (2021–2025)",
       subtitle = "Seasonal Naïve vs Best Holt-Winters",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Consumption (Million Cubic Feet)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Series"))
```

**Interpretation:**

The forecast plot shows that the selected Holt-Winters model captures the main trend and seasonal pattern of U.S. natural gas consumption reasonably well over the test period. The forecasts preserve the strong winter peaks and summer troughs that characterize the series, which is consistent with the earlier conclusion that multiplicative seasonality is appropriate for this dataset. The prediction intervals also widen around the forecast horizon, reflecting increasing uncertainty while still following the recurring seasonal structure.

From the zoomed comparison, the Holt-Winters forecasts track the actual series more closely than the seasonal naïve benchmark in most months. In particular, the Holt-Winters model better captures the magnitude of the large seasonal peaks and generally stays closer to the realized values during both upward and downward movements. By contrast, the seasonal naïve forecast tends to underpredict several high-demand months and does not adjust as effectively to the evolving level of the series.

Overall, these plots provide visual support for the quantitative results reported earlier. The selected Holt-Winters model not only outperforms the seasonal naïve benchmark in RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MASE, but also produces forecasts that align more closely with the observed seasonal dynamics in the test set.

## Residual Diagnostics

```{r}
checkresiduals(hw_mul_fit)
```

**Interpretation:**

The residual diagnostics suggest that the selected multiplicative Holt-Winters model captures much of the overall trend and seasonality, but the residuals are not fully white noise. In the residual time plot, the errors fluctuate around zero without an obvious long-run pattern, which indicates that the model has removed most of the systematic structure in the series.

However, the autocorrelation function shows several significant spikes, and the Ljung-Box test strongly rejects the null hypothesis of no residual autocorrelation (Q* = 65.894, p-value < 0.001). This means that some temporal dependence remains in the residuals, so the model does not completely explain all serial structure in the data. This is not unusual for Holt-Winters models when the series contains additional dynamics beyond smooth trend and seasonality.

The histogram appears roughly centered around zero and is reasonably symmetric, so there is no major evidence of strong bias in the residuals. Overall, the model is still useful and performs well out of sample, but the residual diagnostics suggest that there may still be remaining patterns that a more flexible model could potentially capture.

## Interim Conclusion

The Holt-Winters model provides a natural exponential smoothing approach for capturing trend and seasonality in this series. Among the Holt-Winters candidates, the multiplicative non-damped specification gives the strongest test-set accuracy and clearly outperforms the seasonal naïve benchmark. Although the residual diagnostics indicate that some serial dependence remains, this is not uncommon for Holt-Winters models when the data contain additional dynamics beyond smooth trend and seasonality. Overall, the model provides a strong and interpretable forecasting baseline, even if it does not fully remove all residual structure.

## Conclusion

Overall, the results show that U.S. monthly natural gas consumption is highly predictable using classical time-series methods, largely because the series is driven by a strong long-run upward trend and clear annual seasonality. Across all final candidate models, the Holt-Winters model achieved the best out-of-sample performance on the 24-month test set, outperforming the seasonal naïve benchmark as well as the selected regression and ARIMA models. In particular, the selected multiplicative Holt-Winters specification delivered the lowest RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MASE among all final models, indicating that exponential smoothing with level-dependent seasonality was especially well suited to this dataset.

The seasonal naïve model served as a useful benchmark because it captured the repeating yearly pattern reasonably well, but it could not fully adapt to changes in the overall level of the series. The regression model with linear trend and seasonal dummies also performed strongly and substantially improved on the benchmark, showing that deterministic trend and seasonality explain a large share of the variation in natural gas consumption. However, the Holt-Winters model produced slightly better test-set accuracy, suggesting that a smoothing-based approach was more effective in tracking the evolving level and seasonal magnitude of the series during the forecast period.

The ARIMA model was the weakest among the three main model families considered. Although it explicitly modeled serial dependence, its forecast accuracy was worse than both regression and Holt-Winters. This suggests that, for this dataset, capturing the dominant trend and seasonal structure is more important than adding extra stochastic complexity. From a practical perspective, this is an important result: when forecasting national natural gas demand over the short to medium term, a relatively simple and interpretable seasonal smoothing model may provide more accurate forecasts than more complicated alternatives.

In conclusion, we recommend the multiplicative Holt-Winters model as the final model for this project. It provides the best combination of forecast accuracy, interpretability, and practical value, making it well suited for applications such as energy demand planning, operational decision-making, and policy-oriented forecasting. More broadly, this project shows that classical time-series methods can generate strong and actionable forecasts for U.S. natural gas consumption when the main trend and seasonal patterns are carefully identified and modeled.
